newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judicial group asks Congress for more judges.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judicial group asks Congress for more judges.

text.p: A U.S. judicial group that sets policy for the federal court system voted unanimously Tuesday to ask Congress to create more judgeships for appeals, trials and bankruptcy cases.

The Judicial Conference of the United States, a 27-judge group chaired by Supreme Court Chief Justice William Rehnquist, decided to request that Congress approve the new judgeships because of rapidly increasing workloads.
The group asked that Congress create 12 new appellate court judgeships, a total of 36 trial court judgeships and 18 bankruptcy court judgeships.

But U.S. District Judge William Terrell Hodges of Florida, a member of the group, acknowledged it has unsuccessfully sought more judges from Congress since 1990, and he called the latest request "part of an ongoing process."

Holding a news briefing after the group's semi-annual meeting, he expressed concerned about the number of judicial vacancies yet to be acted upon by Congress, saying it "places a strain on the judicial process."
The latest statistics show 26 vacancies out of 167 federal appeals court judgeships and 67 vacancies out of 647 federal district court judgeships.

"The process has just become more complex from a political standpoint, as well as other considerations," he said in explaining why the judicial vacancies were not being filled. "It's not really new. It's just getting worse."
The Clinton administration has urged the Republican-controlled Senate to approve its judicial nominees.
In other action, the group received an update on legislation it has endorsed to increase judicial pay. The salary for federal judges has been frozen since 1993.
